source_text: Desinat nunc haereticus a Iudaeo, aspis, quod aiunt. a uipera, mutuari uenenum, euomat iam hinc proprii ingenii uirus, phantasma uindicans Christum. nisi quod et in ista sententia alios habebit auctores, praecocos et abortiuos quodammodo Marcionitas, quos apostolus Iohannes antichristos pronuntiauit, negantes Christum in carne uenisse, et tamen non. ut alterius dei ius constituerent, quia et de isto notati fuissent. : sed quoniam incredibile praesumpserant deum carnem. quo magis antichristus Marcion sibi eam rapuit praesumptionem. aptior scilicet ad renuendam corporalem substantiam Christi. qui ipsum deum eius nec auctorem carnis induxerat nec resuscitatorem, optimum uidelicet et in isto et diuersissimum a mendaciis et fallaciis creatoris. et ideo Christus eius, ne mentiretur, ne falleret et hoc modo creatoris forsitan deputaretur. non erat quod uidebatur et quod erat mentiebatur: caro nec caro, homo nec homo. proinde deus, opinor, nec deus. cur enim non etiam dei phantasma portauerit? an credam ei de interiore substantia, qui sit de exteriore frustratus? quomodo uerax habebitur in occulto tam fallax repertus in aperto? quomodo antem, in semetipso ueritatem spiritus, fallaciam carnis confundens, negatam ab apostolo lucis, id est ueritatis, et tenebrarum, id est fallaciae, commisit communicationem? iam nunc. cum mendacium deprehenditur Christi caro, sequitur, ut et omnia, quae per carnem Christi gesta sunt, mendacio gesta sint, congressus contactus conuictus ipsae quoque uirtutes. si enim tangendo aliquem liberauit a uitio uel tactus ab aliquo, quod corporaliter actum est non potest uere actum credi sine corporis ipsius ueritate. nihil solidum ab inani, nihil plenum a uacuo perfici licuit, putatiuus habitus, putatiuus actus: imaginarius operator, imaginariae operae. sic nec passiones Christi eius fidem merebuntur. nihil enim passus est qui non uere est passus; uere autem pati phantasma non potuit. euersum est igitur totum dei opus. totum Christiani nominis et pondus et fructus, mors Christi, negatur, quam tam impresse apostolus demandat, utique ueram, summum eam fundamentum euangelii constituens et salutis nostrae et praedicationis suae. tradidi enim. inquit, uobis in primis, quod Christus mortuus sit pro peccatis nostris et quod sepultus sit et quod resurrexerit tertia die. porro, si caro eius negatur, quomodo mors eius adseueratur, quae propria carnis est passio, per mortem reuertentis in terram, de qua est sumpta, secundum legem sui auctoris? negata uero morte. dum caro negatur, nec de resurrectione constabit. eadem enim ratione non resurrexit, qua mortuus non est, non habendo substantiam scilicet carnis, cuius sicut et mors ita et resurrectio est. proinde resurrectione Christi infirmata etiam nostra i subuersa est. nec ea enim ualebit, propter quam Christus I uenit, si Christi non ualebit. nam sicut illi, qui dicebant resurrectionem mortuorum non esse, reuincuntur ab apostolo ex resurrectione Christi, ita resurrectione Christi non consistente aufertur et mortuorum resurrectio. atque ita inanis I est et fides nostra, inanis et praedicatio apostolorum. inue-: niuntur autem etiam falsi testes dei, quod testimonium dixerint. quasi resuscitauerit Christum, quem non resuscitauit. et sumus adhuc in delictis, et qui in Christo dormierunt. perierunt. sane resurrecturi, sed phantasmate forsitan, sicut et Chiistus.I
pass_a_gloss: Now the heretic ceases to borrow from the Jew, the asp, as they say, from the viper, to mutter its own venom, now the fantasy of Christ is being vindicated. Unless also in this opinion he will have other authors, premature and abortive Marcionites, whom the Apostle John pronounced antichrists, denying Christ came in the flesh, and yet not so that they might establish the right of another god, because they had also been noted for this. But since they had presumed an incredible thing about God, that He is flesh, how much more is Marcion an antichrist, who has seized this presumption for himself, being more suitable for renouncing the bodily substance of Christ, who had not introduced God as the author of flesh nor as the resuscitator, certainly the best and most different from the lies and deceptions of the Creator. And therefore Christ, lest He lie, lest He deceive, and in this way perhaps be considered the Creator, was not what He seemed and what He was, He lied about: flesh was not flesh, man was not man. Accordingly, God, I think, was not God. Why should I not also believe that He bore the fantasy of God? Or should I trust Him about the inner substance, who was deceived about the outer? How will He be considered truthful in secret, when found to be so deceptive in public? How, when confusing truth and falsehood, the Spirit and the flesh, He denied the communication of light, that is, truth, and darkness, that is, falsehood, which the Apostle commended? Now, since the lie about Christ's flesh is detected, it follows that all things that were done through Christ's flesh were done in a lie, the encounters, the contacts, the conversations, even the virtues themselves. For if by touching someone He freed them from vice or was touched by someone, what was done corporally cannot be believed to have been truly done without the truth of the body itself. Nothing solid can be accomplished from nothing, nothing full from emptiness: a pretended habit, pretended actions; an imaginary operator, imaginary works. Thus, Christ's passions will not deserve faith. For He did not suffer what He did not truly suffer; but a fantasy cannot truly suffer. Therefore, the whole work of God is overturned. The whole weight and fruit of the Christian name, Christ's death, is denied, which the Apostle so emphatically demands, certainly true, making it the fundamental basis of the Gospel and our salvation and his own preaching. For I delivered to you, he says, first of all, that Christ died for our sins and that He was buried and that He rose on the third day. Furthermore, if His flesh is denied, how can His death be affirmed, which is a passion proper to flesh, through death returning to the earth, from which it was taken, according to the law of its author? But if death is denied, because flesh is denied, the resurrection will not be established either. For the same reason, He did not rise, as He was not dead, not having the substance of flesh, whose both death and resurrection are. Accordingly, with Christ's resurrection weakened, ours is also overturned. For it will not be valid, for which Christ came, if Christ's is not valid. For just as those who said there is no resurrection of the dead are refuted by the Apostle from Christ's resurrection, so with Christ's resurrection not standing, the resurrection of the dead is also taken away. And so our faith is empty, and the Apostles' preaching is empty. But they are also found to be false witnesses of God, because they said that He raised Christ, whom He did not raise. And we are still in sins, and those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. Indeed, they will rise again, but perhaps as a fantasy, just as Christ.

bible_refs.note: Christ died for our sins and was buried and rose on the third day

pass_b_english: The heretic finally drops the Jew—the asp, they call it, the viper—and stops borrowing venom to spit out his own native poison, now vindicating a phantom Christ. Unless, of course, this opinion has other authors too: premature, abortive Marcionites, whom the apostle John branded antichrists for denying Christ came in the flesh—and yet not so they could establish another god’s right, since they’d already been flagged on that score. But because they presumed the incredible—that God became flesh—Marcion the antichrist seized that very presumption for himself, all the more suited to deny Christ’s bodily substance. After all, this Christ never acknowledged God as either the author of flesh or its resuscitator—the best, obviously, and utterly unlike the Creator’s lies and deceptions. So Christ, to avoid lying, to avoid deceiving, and thus perhaps being mistaken for the Creator, was not what he seemed, and what he was, he lied about: flesh not flesh, man not man. Consequently, God, I reckon, was not God either. Why shouldn’t he also have borne a phantom divinity? Am I to trust him on inner substance when he cheated on the outer? How will he be found truthful in secret when exposed as deceptive in public? How, by confusing truth and falsehood, Spirit and flesh, did he deny the fellowship of light—that is, truth—and darkness—that is, falsehood—which the apostle commended (2 Cor 6:14)? Now that the lie about Christ’s flesh is caught, it follows that everything done through his flesh was done in a lie: the encounters, the contacts, the conversations, even the miracles themselves. If by touching someone he freed them from a defect, or was touched by someone, what was done bodily cannot be believed truly done without the truth of the body itself. Nothing solid comes from nothing, nothing full from emptiness: a simulated habit, simulated acts; an imaginary operator, imaginary works. So his passions earn no faith. He didn’t suffer what he didn’t truly suffer; a phantom cannot truly suffer. The whole work of God is therefore overturned. The entire weight and fruit of the Christian name—Christ’s death—is denied, though the apostle insists on it emphatically as truly real, making it the bedrock of the gospel, our salvation, and his own preaching (1 Cor 15:3-4). For ‘I delivered to you first of all that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day.’ Furthermore, if his flesh is denied, how is his death affirmed—a passion proper to flesh, through death returning to the earth from which it was taken, according to the law of its author? But with death denied because flesh is denied, the resurrection cannot stand either. For the same reason he did not rise, since he did not die, lacking the substance of flesh whose lot is both death and resurrection. Accordingly, with Christ’s resurrection crippled, ours is also overturned. It will not hold, the very thing Christ came for, if Christ’s does not hold. Just as those who said there is no resurrection of the dead are refuted by the apostle from Christ’s resurrection, so with Christ’s resurrection not standing, the resurrection of the dead is also taken away (1 Cor 15:12-13). And so our faith is empty, and the apostles’ preaching empty (1 Cor 15:14). They are even found to be false witnesses of God, since they testified he raised Christ, whom he did not raise (1 Cor 15:15). And we are still in our sins, and those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished (1 Cor 15:17-18). True, they will rise again—but perhaps as a phantom, just like Christ (1 Cor 15:20).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the Marcionite denial of Christ's flesh and the subsequent implications for the resurrection. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the necessary scripture citations (2 Cor 6:14, 1 Cor 15:3-4, 15:12-13, 15:14, 15:15, 15:17-18, 15:20) which are alluded to in the Latin text but not explicitly numbered in the source, fulfilling the requirement for added identifications. Pass A remains a faithful literal gloss.
